record.paper_title: Quasiwypukłość i otwarte problemy analizy funkcjonalnej
record.original_question: Let f be a real-valued function on a space of matrices. Say that f is quasiconvex when it satisfies Morrey's Jensen-type integral inequality for every matrix A and every smooth compactly supported perturbation gradient D phi, and say that f is polyconvex when f(A) can be written as a convex function of all minors of A. Can one give a systematic theory or criterion that decides, for a given quasiconvex function on matrices, whether it is polyconvex?

evidence.quote: Do tej pory nie istnieje uporządkowana teoria pozwalająca stwierdzić, czy dana funkcja quasiwypukła jest poliwypukła.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $M^{m\times n}$ denote the space of real $m\times n$ matrices. A Borel-measurable, locally bounded function $f\colon M^{m\times n}\to\mathbb{R}$ is called **quasiconvex** (in the sense of Morrey) if for every $A\in M^{m\times n}$, every bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, and every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^m)$,
$$\int_\Omega f(A+D\varphi(x))\,dx \;\ge\; |\Omega|\,f(A).$$
The function $f$ is called **polyconvex** if there exists a convex function $g\colon\mathbb{R}^{\tau(m,n)}\to\mathbb{R}$ such that
$$f(A) \;=\; g(T(A)) \qquad\text{for all } A\in M^{m\times n},$$
where $T(A)$ is the vector of all minors (subdeterminants of all orders) of $A$ and $\tau(m,n)$ is their total number.

It is classical that polyconvexity implies quasiconvexity, and that the converse fails in general (for instance, in dimensions $m=n=2$ there exist quasiconvex functions that are not polyconvex).

**Problem.** Develop a systematic theory, or provide an effective criterion, that decides for an arbitrary given quasiconvex function $f\colon M^{m\times n}\to\mathbb{R}$ whether or not $f$ is polyconvex.
artifact.category_tag: Quasiconvex and polyconvex functions in the calculus of variations
artifact.status_search_result: No systematic theory or decidable criterion is known for determining when a quasiconvex function on matrices is polyconvex. While the strict implications among the convexity hierarchy (convex ⇒ polyconvex ⇒ quasiconvex ⇒ rank-one convex) are well established and explicit examples of quasiconvex non-polyconvex functions exist (e.g. Šverák's 2D example), characterizing polyconvexity inside the quasiconvex class remains an outstanding problem in the vectorial calculus of variations, closely tied to the still-open planar Morrey conjecture.

status_evidence.snippet: convex ⇒ polyconvex ⇒ quasiconvex ⇒ rank-one convex; the planar Morrey conjecture remains open.
status_evidence.claim: The relations among convexity notions and the open status of related problems are documented.

status_evidence.title: An example of a quasiconvex function that is not polyconvex in two dimensions
status_evidence.snippet: Constructs a quasiconvex function on 2x2 matrices that is not polyconvex.
status_evidence.claim: Quasiconvex ⇏ polyconvex even in two dimensions; no general criterion is provided.

status_evidence.title: Quasiconvexity and its role in the Calculus of Variations
status_evidence.snippet: Characterizing quasiconvex and polyconvex functions remains a central problem in vectorial calculus of variations.
status_evidence.claim: No general systematic theory deciding polyconvexity of a given quasiconvex function is available.
